headline: Ateru is from Old Japanese 当つ (atu), in the lower bigrade pattern.

sources.quote: From Old Japanese 当つ (atu), following 下二段活用 (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”).
Development

Natural progression from Old and Classical Japanese 下(しも)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”) verbs ending in -u to modern Japanese 下(しも)一(いち)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo ichidan katsuyō, “lower monograde conjugation”) verbs ending in -eru.

sources.quote: From Old Japanese 劣る (oto₂ru), from Proto-Japonic *ətəru, from Proto-Japonic *ət-.

headline: Manabu is 真似 (mana, “imitating, copying”) plus ぶ (-bu, “to seem like, to act like”): “to learn” as “to imitate”.

sources.quote: From 真似(まな) (mana, “imitating, copying”) + ぶ (-bu, “to seem like, to act like”, verb-forming suffix). Cognate with 学ぶ (manebu).

The initial mana might be a phonetic shift from mane, itself the continuative or stem nominal form of classical verb 真似 (manu, “to imitate, to copy”), from 真 (ma-, “true, real”) + 似 (nu, “copy, imitate”, lower bigrade conjugation; not attested in isolation).
First cited in the Nihon Shoki of 720.

The ぶ (-bu) suffix usually conjugated with the upper bigrade pattern (上(かみ)二(に)段活用(だんかつよう) (kami nidan katsuyō)), and manabu conjugated this way until the early Heian period (early 800s). Starting from the mid-Heian (roughly the 900s or 1000s), manabu shifted to conjugate using the classical yodan pattern, the precursor to the modern godan conjugation (五段活用(ごだんかつよう) (godan katsuyō)).
